endpoints.interpretation: Cumulative removal of PFOA from aqueous solution over successive IX adsorption cycles with regeneration at 30 mM PDS was evaluated to demonstrate the cyclic treatment performance; cumulative PFOA removal increased linearly with cycle number for regenerated resins.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS were desorbed from loaded anion exchange resins into regenerant brine/cosolvent solutions. Conventional regenerable AERs achieved near-complete PFAS desorption with 10 bed volumes of 70% methanolic brine, while PFAS-selective resins required 30 bed volumes of higher methanol content (90%) or more hydrophobic cosolvent (n-propanol) brines. The endpoint is PFAS transfer from solid resin to liquid regenerant, enabling resin reuse rather than PFAS destruction.

Cationically Modified PVA-Based Electrospun Nanofiber Membrane for Adsorptive PFAS Removal from Water. ACS Applied Engineering Materials. 2026;4:93-106. doi:10.1021/acsaenm.5c00822.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale batch adsorption–regeneration using a defined PVA-CTAC ENM adsorbent, mixed PFAS aqueous solution, standardized regenerant chemistry (1% methanolic NH4OH), and clearly defined cycle number and recovery/removal endpoints makes this record reasonably comparable to other bench-scale PFAS adsorbent regeneration studies that report percent recovery or capacity retention over cycles. However, exact PFAS concentrations, water matrix (for regeneration), and per-compound numeric cycle data are not fully specified in the provided text and would need alignment when making detailed quantitative comparisons.

endpoints.interpretation: Mass of PFAS desorbed into methanolic NH4OH regenerant (recovery) relative to PFAS adsorbed, across three adsorption–desorption cycles; several PFAS showed recovery consistently at or above 95%, indicating efficient desorption and media regeneration.
PFAS removal efficiencies from water (R%) by regenerated PVA-CTAC ENM remained high over three cycles, with little variation for most PFAS, indicating sustained adsorption capacity upon reuse.

Study emphasized ENM regenerability and reusability obtained through cross-linking; authors note potential pore blockage affecting PFHxS removal in later cycles and speculate that initially inaccessible sites for PFOS became available after the first regeneration; no post-regeneration FTIR/XPS was performed to confirm structural changes.

limitations.statement: Regeneration and reuse were evaluated only for three adsorption–desorption cycles, and detailed compound-specific recovery and removal data are reported in a supplementary table not available in the provided text.
Post-regeneration FTIR or XPS characterization to confirm structural or chemical changes upon reuse was not performed, and the authors note that future studies will include these analyses.

endpoints.interpretation: LCA evaluates how replacing NaCl with alternative salts and adding inorganic bases at 0.5% (m/m) affects climate change, human toxicity, ecotoxicity, and eutrophication impacts relative to NaCl-based regeneration, considering differences between salts produced chemically versus by natural processes.
endpoints.reported_term: life cycle environmental impacts of alternative salt and base regeneration

endpoints.interpretation: Study interprets increased environmental impacts from alternative salts and inorganic bases against their potential to enable future coupling of regeneration with PFAS destruction technologies such as electrochemical oxidation (sulfate-based solutions) or hydrothermal treatment (alkaline solutions).
endpoints.reported_term: trade-offs and coupling potential with PFAS destruction technologies

limitations.statement: All alternative salt and base regeneration options are hypothetical and use generic life cycle inventory data for salts and bases; actual PFAS desorption efficiency, AER performance with alternative mobile counterions, and compatibility with downstream destruction technologies are not experimentally verified within this study.

The LCA shows that all non-NaCl salts and inorganic bases considered have greater environmental impacts than NaCl, particularly when derived from chemical production, but does not evaluate whether potential benefits from integration with PFAS destruction technologies would offset these higher impacts.

S12-E05 describes high PFAS mass loadings on resins at the end of the pilot, implying concentrated residual PFAS on the media. However, the specific management options for the spent pilot resins (off-site regeneration, disposal, incineration) and the statement that these options were 'implied but not experimentally investigated' are not explicitly addressed. The existence of concentrated PFAS on spent media is supported; the management-options language is inferred.

S12-E03 refers to a 'field pilot' design with multiple AER columns, and S12-E08 notes that the pilot test was performed at a source zone site. This supports the description of a field pilot-scale ion exchange column system operating on contaminated groundwater at a source-zone site.

S12-E03 describes evaluation of regenerable vs single-use resins, S12-E05–E06 distinguish 'single-use AERs' and 'regenerable AERs', and S12-E06 Table 3 lists the resins A860, A520E, PFA694E, CalRes 2301, and PSR2+. This supports that regenerable and single-use AERs were compared in fixed-bed columns for PFAS removal. However, the assertion that A860 and A520E specifically are the regenerable resins is not established in the provided excerpts; that mapping between resin identity and regenerability is not shown here. Thus the core treatment description is supported, but the specific identification of which resins are regenerable is not fully supported.

Therefore, the record is usable with minor qualifier caveats.

comparability.reason: The study provides modeled breakthrough behavior, O&M cost multipliers, and qualitative rules for routing PFAS-loaded GAC to reactivation versus HTI under specific WRRF-scale design and regulatory assumptions. It does not report empirical regeneration efficiencies, capacity recovery over cycles, or destruction efficiencies, so results are best used qualitatively to inform relative costs of media replacement versus reactivation/incineration rather than quantitatively compared with laboratory adsorption–regeneration experiments.

endpoints.interpretation: Modeled separation of PFAS from WRRF effluent by GAC/AIX adsorbers, characterized by time or bed volumes to breakthrough at 5 ng/L, used to estimate media usage and O&M costs.

limitations.statement: Modeling is based on assumed influent PFBA and PFBS concentrations, simplified breakthrough criteria (5 ng/L), and statewide average conditions; authors note substantial design uncertainties and the need for full-scale testing to ensure consistent PFAS removal and destruction at WRRFs.

Temporal variability in PFAS loading to WRRFs (requiring up to nine daily grab samples for characterization in other work) limits accuracy of media changeout frequency predictions and complicates compliance with low-level PFAS effluent limits.

Cost and design assumptions for media destruction focus only on two technologies currently available at WRRF-relevant scale (GAC reactivation and HTI); other destruction options may emerge with different capital and O&M costs.

The analysis assumes that GAC from facilities with design flowrates >1 MGD will be sent to site-dedicated reactivation, while smaller facilities use HTI; this threshold is based on vendor discussions and may not reflect all market conditions.

Results represent facilities with minimal industrial PFAS inputs; WRRFs with significant industrial PFAS loads may need more frequent media changeout and/or additional vessels, increasing capital and O&M costs beyond modeled ranges.
